titulo.texto: Zoomorphic Vessel The Duck of Tlatilco

frase_gancho.texto: A black clay duck that recalls when the valley was a lake.

puente_narrativo.texto: Stay with the water: the next vessel is a fish, another inhabitant of the lakes that fed the village.

guion_corto.texto: This duck of burnished black clay is a vessel: the bird’s round body holds the liquid, and an opening lets you pour it out. It was made in Tlatilco more than three thousand years ago, when the Valley of Mexico was a network of lakes and reed beds where thousands of migratory birds arrived every winter. Notice how simple and elegant it is: a few scraped lines suggest the wings and the neck, with no needless ornament. The black shine comes from firing without oxygen and from patient polishing. For these people the lake was not scenery; it was pantry, calendar and mystery. And this duck was a way of giving thanks.

guion_largo.texto:
Close your eyes for a moment and imagine the Valley of Mexico on a winter morning, three thousand years ago. There are no streets or buildings: there is water. Five great lakes, reed beds, small islands, and above them all, thousands of ducks that have just arrived from the north. That spectacle repeated itself every year, and it still does, with fewer ducks, in what remains of Xochimilco. For the people of Tlatilco, that return was a sign that the year was turning.

The lake was their supermarket. From it they took fish, frogs, insects, plants and, above all, birds. Centuries later, the Mexica would still hunt ducks with nets and darts, and Tenochtitlan would feed on what came out of the lagoon. This vessel lets us glimpse the beginning of that story. And the people of the lake did not live on ducks alone: the Mexica would eat axolotls, which still exist in Xochimilco, though in danger of disappearing; ahuautle, which is the tiny eggs of water flies and is called “Mexican caviar”; and a foamy algae that they dried into cakes. The lake gave everything.

Now look at its technique. The clay of Tlatilco was smoothed with a small stone until it had that mirror shine, and then it was fired in a low-oxygen fire, which blackens the surface. It is the technique of polished black clay, highly prized in Tlatilco and still alive today: upstairs, in the Oaxaca Hall, you will see the famous black pottery of San Bartolo Coyotepec, which follows that tradition. And observe the shape: the bird’s body becomes a container, and the scraped lines suggest wings and neck. The beauty lies in what is not added.

The people of Tlatilco made many containers in the shape of animals: fish, turtles, rabbits, ducks and dogs, among them the xoloitzcuintles, the hairless dogs. Those dogs were important for centuries: the Mexica believed they accompanied the dead on their journey to Mictlán. Perhaps in Tlatilco they already saw them in a similar way: there are tombs in which the dog lies beside the deceased.

There is also a clue to connect this piece with others. When you reach the Mexica Hall, look at the wind god, Ehécatl. He was represented with a mask in the shape of a bird’s beak, which many describe as a duck’s bill. And the bronze conch shell in the courtyard is also his emblem. In other words: the birds of the lake, from the lagoon of Tlatilco to the Mexica gods, were always very close to the wind.

And a fact that will surprise you: even today, in the lakes of Chapultepec Forest, a few steps from the museum, migratory ducks arrive every winter. If you go for a stroll after your visit, you may see the descendants of those that inspired this vessel come gliding down.

And one last lesson from this vessel: the everyday can also be sacred. A duck for drinking, a duck for offering. The same piece served at the table and in the beyond, and in that blend of the useful and the ritual lies the whole spirit of this village.

texto.Dimensions: 0.21 m high x 0.125 m wide x 0.19 m long

texto.pregunta: Myth: The shiny black clay is enamel or modern paint.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The shine is achieved by polishing the clay with a stone and firing it without oxygen; it is a technique that has been used in the valley for more than three thousand years.
